questions.q: Who created Linux, and when?
questions.a: Linus Torvalds, a Finnish student, announced the first Linux kernel (version 0.01) in September 1991. He still leads kernel development today.

questions.q: What is the difference between Linux and a Linux distribution?
questions.a: Linux is only the kernel - the core that manages CPU, memory, devices and processes. A distribution (Ubuntu, Fedora, Debian) bundles the kernel with GNU tools, libraries, a package manager and apps to make a complete, usable OS.

questions.q: Which license is the Linux kernel released under?
questions.a: GNU GPL version 2 (GPL-2.0-only), with a syscall exception so normal programs that just use Linux system calls do not have to be GPL themselves.

questions.q: What does GNU stand for, and why does it matter to Linux?
questions.a: GNU stands for "GNU's Not Unix". Richard Stallman started the GNU Project in 1983 to build a free Unix-like OS. GNU supplied the tools (gcc, bash, coreutils) that, combined with the Linux kernel, make a full system - hence the name GNU/Linux.

questions.q: What is the kernel's main job?
questions.a: It manages the hardware for every program: CPU scheduling, memory management, device drivers, filesystems and networking. Programs request these services through system calls instead of touching hardware directly.

questions.q: What is the difference between Unix and Linux?
questions.a: Unix is the original proprietary OS family started at Bell Labs in 1969. Linux is a free, open-source Unix-like kernel written from scratch; it follows Unix design and POSIX conventions but contains no Unix source code.

questions.q: What is a shell?
questions.a: A command-line interpreter between you and the OS. It reads commands, starts programs and provides scripting features like variables, loops and pipes. Bash is the most common Linux shell.

questions.q: Name some popular Linux distributions and their families.
questions.a: Debian family: Debian, Ubuntu, Linux Mint (they use apt and .deb packages). Red Hat family: RHEL, CentOS Stream, Fedora (they use dnf and .rpm packages). Others: Arch, openSUSE, Alpine.

questions.q: What is the difference between kernel space and user space?
questions.a: Kernel space is where the kernel runs with full hardware access. User space is where normal programs run with restricted access; for privileged work like file or network access they must ask the kernel through a system call.

questions.q: Why is Linux so popular for servers?
questions.a: It is free and open source, stable for years of uptime, secure by design (users, permissions, fast patches), runs on almost any hardware, and is easy to automate with shells and tools. Most cloud and web servers run Linux.

questions.q: How is Windows different from Linux?
questions.a: Windows is a commercial operating system made by Microsoft. Linux is free and open source, and it is more secure, stable, and widely used for servers.

questions.q: What is one feature Linux has but Windows does not?
questions.a: Linux is fully open source, so anyone can see and modify its code. This gives complete control and customization that Windows does not allow.

questions.q: What is Linux?
questions.a: Linux is a free, open-source operating system kernel based on Unix. Combined with system tools in a distribution, it powers most servers, Android phones, and cloud systems.

questions.q: What is an Operating System (OS)?
questions.a: An Operating System is software that manages the computer's hardware and software resources. It acts as a bridge between the user and the hardware.

questions.q: What is Bash?
questions.a: Bash (Bourne Again Shell) is the default command-line shell in most Linux distributions. It is used to run commands and to write shell scripts.

questions.q: What is the difference between CLI and GUI?
questions.a: CLI (Command Line Interface) lets you work by typing commands. GUI (Graphical User Interface) lets you work with windows, icons, and menus.

questions.q: What is the difference between the Kernel and the Shell?
questions.a: The Kernel talks directly to the hardware and manages system resources. The Shell is the interface through which the user gives commands to the Kernel.

questions.q: What is the difference between RHEL and Ubuntu?
questions.a: RHEL uses RPM packages with dnf/yum and is enterprise-focused with paid support. Ubuntu uses DEB packages with apt and is community-focused and free.

questions.q: What is the difference between CentOS and RHEL?
questions.a: RHEL is a commercial distribution with official Red Hat support. CentOS was its free community rebuild; today CentOS Stream sits just ahead of RHEL development.

questions.q: Which Linux distribution do you like, and why?
questions.a: Sample answer: RHEL, because it is stable, secure, and widely used in enterprise environments with long-term support.

questions.q: Have you explored the Linux kernel?
questions.a: Sample answer: Yes. I understand that the kernel manages hardware, memory, processes, and device drivers, and I use commands like uname and dmesg to see kernel information.

questions.q: What is the difference between an absolute and a relative path?
questions.a: An absolute path starts from the root / (for example /home/akash/file.txt) and means the same thing from anywhere. A relative path is resolved from your current directory (docs/file.txt) and changes meaning as you cd around.

questions.q: What do . and .. mean in a directory listing?
questions.a: . refers to the current directory and .. to the parent directory. They are real directory entries, so commands like cd .. move you up one level and ./script runs a script in the current directory.

questions.q: How do you see your current directory and jump to your home directory?
questions.a: pwd prints the current directory. cd with no argument (or cd ~) takes you to your home directory, which is stored in the $HOME variable.

questions.q: What is the difference between ls, ls -l and ls -a?
questions.a: ls lists names only. ls -l shows the long format: permissions, link count, owner, group, size and modification time. ls -a also shows hidden files - names starting with a dot, including . and ..

questions.q: What is the root directory and what lives directly under it?
questions.a: / is the top of the single filesystem tree. Standard children: /etc (configuration), /home (user data), /var (logs and changing data), /usr (programs and libraries), /bin and /sbin (essential commands), /tmp (temporary files), /dev (device files), /proc and /sys (kernel information).

questions.q: What are /proc and /sys?
questions.a: Virtual filesystems the kernel exposes as files. /proc shows process and system information (for example /proc/cpuinfo); /sys exposes devices and kernel objects for tools like udev. Nothing there is a real disk file.

questions.q: How is cd - useful?
questions.a: cd - jumps back to the previous directory you were in and prints it. It is the fastest way to toggle between two directories.

questions.q: What is a hidden file in Linux?
questions.a: Any file whose name begins with a dot, like .bashrc. It is not secret or protected - it is simply not shown by default; ls -a reveals it. Dotfiles in your home directory store per-user configuration.

questions.q: What does the tilde (~) expand to?
questions.a: Your home directory: ~/docs means /home/akash/docs. The form ~name expands to that user's home directory, for example ~root is /root.

questions.q: What is the difference between cp a b and mv a b?
questions.a: cp copies, so the original stays in place. mv renames or moves, so the original path no longer exists. Across filesystems mv actually copies and then deletes the original.

questions.q: What is the purpose of /etc, /var, /home, /tmp, /opt, /usr, /boot, /dev, /proc and /sys?
questions.a: /etc stores configuration files. /var stores changing data like logs. /home stores users' personal files. /tmp stores temporary files. /opt stores optional third-party software. /usr stores commands, libraries, and applications. /boot stores bootloader and kernel files. /dev contains device files. /proc shows process and kernel information. /sys shows hardware and kernel object information.

questions.q: What is the difference between a file and a directory?
questions.a: A file stores data. A directory is a container that stores files and other directories.

questions.q: How do you create an empty file or update a file's timestamp?
questions.a: touch filename. It creates the file if it is missing; if it exists, it updates the access and modification times to now.

questions.q: What is the difference between a hard link and a symbolic (soft) link?
questions.a: A hard link is another name for the same inode - the same data - so it survives deletion of the other names, but it cannot cross filesystems or point to a directory. A symlink is a small file containing a path: it can cross filesystems and point to directories, but it breaks if the target is deleted.

questions.q: Which commands show disk usage?
questions.a: df -h shows free and used space per mounted filesystem. du -sh * shows the size of each item in the current directory in human-readable form. ncdu (if installed) gives an interactive browser.

questions.q: How do you create a directory together with its parents in one step?
questions.a: mkdir -p /a/b/c creates any missing parent directories and does not complain if some already exist.

questions.q: What does rm -r do, and why is rm -rf dangerous?
questions.a: rm -r deletes directories and everything inside them, recursively. Adding -f forces the deletion without prompts and ignores missing files, so a single typo can silently destroy the wrong directory tree or even the whole system.

questions.q: How do you copy a whole directory tree?
questions.a: cp -r source dest copies recursively. cp -a (archive mode) also preserves permissions, ownership and timestamps, which is what you want for backups.

questions.q: How do you find a file by name under a directory?
questions.a: find /path -name 'file.txt'. Useful variants: -iname for case-insensitive matching, -type f or -type d, and -mtime -7 for files changed in the last 7 days.

questions.q: What is the difference between find and locate?
questions.a: find searches the live filesystem, so it is slower but always current. locate searches a prebuilt database (refreshed by updatedb), so it is instant but can miss very new files or still list deleted ones.

questions.q: What does the file command do?
questions.a: file name inspects the file's actual contents (magic bytes) and reports its real type - text, ELF binary, image, archive - no matter what extension the name has.

questions.q: How do you rename many files at once?
questions.a: The usual approach is a shell loop: for f in *.txt; do mv "$f" "${f%.txt}.bak"; done. Some distros also ship a rename command. Plain mv has no batch renaming syntax.

questions.q: What is the Linux equivalent of a Windows .exe file?
questions.a: Linux does not depend on extensions. Any file with execute permission can run as a program, and shell scripts (.sh) are the common equivalent for tools and installers.

questions.q: How do you compress and extract files?
questions.a: Use tar: tar -czvf archive.tar.gz folder/ creates a compressed archive, and tar -xzvf archive.tar.gz extracts it. For .zip files, use zip and unzip.

questions.q: What is the difference between cat, less, head and tail?
questions.a: cat dumps whole files to stdout - fine for small files or joining files. less pages through big files interactively with search. head shows the first lines (10 by default), tail the last; tail -f follows a growing file live, the classic way to watch logs.

questions.q: How do you search for text inside files?
questions.a: grep 'pattern' file. Common flags: -r recursive into directories, -i case-insensitive, -n show line numbers, -v invert (show non-matching lines), -c just count matches.

questions.q: What is a pipe?
questions.a: The | operator sends one command's standard output into the next command's standard input, for example ps aux | grep nginx. Chaining small tools this way is the core Unix philosophy.

questions.q: What is the difference between > and >>?
questions.a: > redirects stdout to a file and overwrites it; >> appends instead. Both create the file if it does not exist. The related form 2> redirects stderr.

questions.q: How do you count lines, words and bytes in a file?
questions.a: wc file prints lines, words and bytes; wc -l gives only the line count. A typical use: grep ERROR app.log | wc -l to count error lines.

questions.q: What does sort do, and how do you get unique lines?
questions.a: sort orders lines alphabetically; -n sorts numerically, -r reverses, -k selects a column. uniq removes only ADJACENT duplicate lines, so the standard idiom is sort file | uniq, or simply sort -u.

questions.q: How do you see the differences between two files?
questions.a: diff file1 file2 shows the changed lines; diff -u produces the unified format used in patches. For side-by-side comparison use diff -y or vimdiff.

questions.q: What are cut, awk and sed used for?
questions.a: cut extracts columns by a delimiter: cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd. awk splits lines into fields and processes them: awk '{print $1}'. sed edits streams, most often search-and-replace: sed 's/old/new/g' file (add -i to edit the file in place).

questions.q: How do you watch a log file in real time?
questions.a: tail -f /var/log/syslog, or journalctl -f on systemd systems. New lines appear as they are written; Ctrl+C stops following.

questions.q: How do you find which files under /etc contain a string?
questions.a: grep -r 'string' /etc. Add -l to list only the matching filenames, or -n to include line numbers with each match.

questions.q: What do the fields in an ls -l permission string like -rwxr-xr-- mean?
questions.a: The first character is the type (- file, d directory, l symlink). Then come three triplets: owner, group, others. In each triplet r = read (4), w = write (2), x = execute (1). So rwxr-xr-- is owner rwx, group r-x, others r-- - octal 754.

questions.q: How do you change permissions with chmod?
questions.a: Symbolic form: chmod u+x file, chmod g-w file. Octal form: chmod 755 file gives the owner rwx and everyone else r-x. On directories, x means 'allowed to enter'.

questions.q: What is the difference between chmod, chown and chgrp?
questions.a: chmod changes the permission bits. chown changes the owner, and optionally the group too: chown user:group file. chgrp changes only the group. You need to be root or the file's owner.

questions.q: Where are user accounts and groups stored?
questions.a: Account information lives in /etc/passwd; password hashes live in /etc/shadow, readable only by root. Groups are defined in /etc/group, with /etc/gshadow for group passwords and admins.

questions.q: How do you add a user and give them sudo rights?
questions.a: Create the account with adduser name (Debian/Ubuntu) or useradd name plus passwd name. Then add them to the admin group: usermod -aG sudo name on Debian/Ubuntu, or the wheel group on RHEL/Fedora.

questions.q: What is the root user, and what is sudo?
questions.a: root (UID 0) is the superuser that bypasses permission checks. sudo lets permitted users run single commands as root, with every use logged - much safer than working as root all the time.

questions.q: What does the id command show?
questions.a: Your numeric uid, your primary gid, and every group you belong to - for example uid=1000(akash) gid=1000(akash) groups=1000(akash),27(sudo).

questions.q: What is the difference between su and sudo?
questions.a: su switches to another account (root by default) and asks for the TARGET account's password. sudo runs one command as root, asks for YOUR password, checks the sudoers policy, and logs the action.

questions.q: How do you lock or delete a user account?
questions.a: Lock the password with usermod -L name (or passwd -l name). Delete the account with userdel name; add -r to also remove the home directory and mail spool.

questions.q: What are the SUID, SGID and sticky bits?
questions.a: Special permission bits: SUID (octal 4xxx) runs a program with the file owner's rights - passwd is the classic example. SGID (2xxx) does the same with the group, and on a directory makes new files inherit the directory's group. The sticky bit (1xxx) on a shared directory like /tmp means only a file's owner can delete it.

questions.q: What is the difference between useradd and adduser?
questions.a: useradd is the low-level command with basic options. adduser is a friendlier script on Debian/Ubuntu that creates the home directory and applies defaults automatically.

questions.q: How do you add a user to a group?
questions.a: Use usermod -aG groupname username. The -a option appends the group; without it, the user's other group memberships would be replaced.

questions.q: How do you change a user's password?
questions.a: Use passwd username and enter the new password. A user changes their own password with plain passwd; root can change anyone's.

questions.q: What are primary and secondary groups?
questions.a: A primary group is the user's default group, which new files they create belong to. Secondary groups give the user extra permissions to shared resources.

questions.q: What is the difference between a user and a group?
questions.a: A user is an individual account used to log in to the system. A group is a collection of users that makes managing permissions easier.

questions.q: Why do we use groups in Linux?
questions.a: Groups let you manage permissions for many users at the same time. This makes administration easier and more secure.

questions.q: How do you give a file only read and write permission?
questions.a: Use chmod 600 filename. This gives the owner read and write (rw-) and removes all permissions for group and others.

questions.q: How do you see which processes are running?
questions.a: ps aux for a one-time snapshot of all processes; top or htop for a live, sorted view; pgrep name to find the PID of a process by name.

questions.q: What are PID and PPID?
questions.a: PID is the process ID the kernel assigns to each process; PPID is its parent's PID. PID 1 - systemd on most distros - is the first process at boot and the ancestor of everything else.

questions.q: How do you stop a process?
questions.a: kill PID sends SIGTERM (15), a polite request to exit that allows cleanup. kill -9 PID sends SIGKILL, which the process cannot catch or ignore - a last resort, because it gets no chance to clean up. pkill and killall work by name instead of PID.

questions.q: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
questions.a: A process has its own private memory space; threads are tasks inside a process that share its memory, so they are cheaper to create but can interfere with each other's data.

questions.q: What is a daemon?
questions.a: A background service process that runs detached from any terminal - for example sshd or cron. On modern distros daemons are normally started and supervised by systemd as service units.

questions.q: How do you run a command in the background and bring it back?
questions.a: Append & to start it in the background. jobs lists the shell's jobs, fg %1 brings one to the foreground, Ctrl+Z suspends a foreground job, and bg %1 resumes it in the background. To survive logout use nohup, tmux, or a systemd service.

questions.q: What is a zombie process?
questions.a: A process that has finished but whose parent has not yet collected its exit status with wait(). It keeps only a process-table entry and no memory. The real fix is to signal or restart the misbehaving parent; orphaned zombies are reaped by PID 1.

questions.q: How do you find which process is using a file or a port?
questions.a: lsof /path/to/file shows processes with that file open; lsof -i :80 shows what holds port 80. ss -tulpen maps listening sockets to processes (run as root to see other users' processes).

questions.q: What do nice and renice do?
questions.a: They adjust CPU scheduling priority. Nice values run from -20 (highest priority, root only) to 19 (lowest). nice -n 10 command starts a program at lower priority; renice changes the priority of an already-running process.

questions.q: What is the difference between SIGTERM and SIGKILL?
questions.a: SIGTERM (15) asks the process to shut down and can be caught or ignored, so the process can clean up first. SIGKILL (9) is enforced by the kernel directly: the process dies immediately with no cleanup.

questions.q: What is a process?
questions.a: A process is a running instance of a program. Every process gets a unique Process ID (PID) from the kernel.

questions.q: What is the difference between a process and a service?
questions.a: A process is any running program. A service is a background process that provides system or application functionality, like sshd or Apache.

questions.q: What is an orphan process?
questions.a: An orphan is a running process whose parent has already terminated. It is automatically adopted by PID 1 (init or systemd).

questions.q: What is the difference between foreground and background processes?
questions.a: A foreground process runs in the terminal and accepts user input. A background process runs independently without blocking the terminal.

questions.q: What are parent and child processes?
questions.a: A parent process is one that creates another process. The new process is called the child, and it runs independently but is initially managed by its parent.

questions.q: What is the difference between apt, apt-get and dpkg?
questions.a: dpkg installs individual .deb files but does not resolve dependencies. apt and apt-get work with repositories and handle dependencies automatically; apt is the friendlier modern command (apt install, apt update), apt-get is the older script-stable interface.

questions.q: What do apt update and apt upgrade actually do?
questions.a: apt update only downloads the latest package INDEX from the repositories - it installs nothing. apt upgrade then installs the newer versions of your installed packages. The correct order is update first, then upgrade.

questions.q: How do you find, install and remove a package on Debian/Ubuntu?
questions.a: apt search keyword to find it, apt show name for details, sudo apt install name to install it, and sudo apt remove name to uninstall (apt purge also deletes its configuration files).

questions.q: What are the equivalents on RHEL/Fedora systems?
questions.a: dnf, the modern replacement for yum: dnf search, dnf install, dnf remove, dnf update. These manage .rpm packages; rpm -ivh installs a single downloaded package without resolving dependencies.

questions.q: What is a package repository?
questions.a: A server that hosts packages plus signed metadata about them. Your system fetches from the repositories listed in /etc/apt/sources.list and /etc/apt/sources.list.d (Debian/Ubuntu) or /etc/yum.repos.d (RHEL/Fedora).

questions.q: What is a dependency?
questions.a: Another package a program needs in order to run - libraries, interpreters, helper tools. apt and dnf install dependencies automatically; dpkg and rpm alone do not, which is the main reason the higher-level tools exist.

questions.q: How do you list installed packages and find which package owns a file?
questions.a: On Debian/Ubuntu: dpkg -l lists installed packages and dpkg -S /path/to/file names the owning package. On RHEL/Fedora: rpm -qa lists them and rpm -qf /path/to/file names the owner.

questions.q: What are snap and flatpak?
questions.a: Distribution-independent package formats that bundle their dependencies and run sandboxed. Snaps come from Canonical's store; flatpaks usually come from Flathub. They trade extra disk space for portability across distros.

questions.q: How do you compile software from source, in short?
questions.a: The classic flow is ./configure (checks your system and generates a Makefile), make (compiles), then sudo make install (copies files, usually under /usr/local). You need a compiler and the relevant -dev libraries installed first.

questions.q: How do you fix 'Unable to locate package' on Ubuntu?
questions.a: Run sudo apt update first - the local package index is missing or stale. If it still fails, either the package name is wrong (check with apt search) or the repository that carries it (universe, multiverse, or a PPA) is not enabled.

questions.q: What is RPM?
questions.a: RPM (Red Hat Package Manager) is the package format used by RHEL-based distributions. The rpm command installs and manages individual .rpm package files.

questions.q: What is the difference between RPM and YUM/DNF?
questions.a: rpm installs individual package files but does not resolve dependencies. YUM and DNF work with repositories and install dependencies automatically.

questions.q: What is the difference between MySQL and MariaDB?
questions.a: MariaDB is a community-driven fork of MySQL. It is fully open source and offers extra features and performance improvements.

questions.q: How do you check your IP address and routing table?
questions.a: ip addr shows interfaces and their addresses; ip route shows the routing table, including the default gateway. The older equivalents are ifconfig and route -n.

questions.q: How do you test connectivity step by step?
questions.a: Ping your gateway first, then an external IP like 8.8.8.8, then a name like google.com. If the IP works but the name fails, the problem is DNS; if even the gateway fails, the problem is the local link or Wi-Fi.

questions.q: What is DNS and where is it configured?
questions.a: DNS resolves hostnames to IP addresses. Clients query the resolvers listed in /etc/resolv.conf (often managed by systemd-resolved or NetworkManager today). The static /etc/hosts file is consulted before DNS.

questions.q: How do you see which ports are listening on a machine?
questions.a: ss -tuln lists listening TCP and UDP sockets numerically; add -p (as root) to see the process behind each one. The older equivalent is netstat -tulpn.

questions.q: What is the difference between TCP and UDP?
questions.a: TCP is connection-oriented: ordered, acknowledged and retransmitted delivery - used by the web and SSH. UDP is connectionless: no delivery guarantee or ordering, but very low overhead - used by DNS queries, DHCP and voice/video.

questions.q: How do you test whether a remote port is open?
questions.a: nc -zv host port does a direct check; telnet host port also works. For a web service, curl -Iv https://host tests the whole stack including DNS and TLS.

questions.q: What does the /etc/hosts file do?
questions.a: It maps names to IP addresses locally and is checked before DNS. Each line is an IP followed by one or more names, for example 127.0.0.1 localhost. It is handy for overrides and for blocking names by pointing them at 127.0.0.1.

questions.q: What is a default gateway?
questions.a: The router your machine forwards traffic to when the destination is outside the local network. It appears as 'default via ...' in the output of ip route.

questions.q: How do you download a file from the command line?
questions.a: curl -O URL saves it under the remote name; wget URL does the same. curl is also the standard tool for testing HTTP APIs: curl -s https://api.example.com.

questions.q: What is the difference between ssh and scp?
questions.a: ssh opens an encrypted remote shell: ssh user@host. scp copies files over the same encrypted channel: scp file user@host:/path. sftp is the interactive file-transfer variant, and rsync over ssh is better for large or repeated syncs.

questions.q: What is an IP address?
questions.a: An IP address is a unique address assigned to a device on a network. It allows devices to find and communicate with each other.

questions.q: What is the difference between IPv4 and IPv6?
questions.a: IPv4 is a 32-bit address (like 192.168.1.10) and is the most common. IPv6 is a 128-bit address created to solve the IPv4 address shortage.

questions.q: What is a subnet mask?
questions.a: A subnet mask separates the network part from the host part of an IP address. It tells whether two devices are in the same network.

questions.q: What is DHCP?
questions.a: DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) automatically assigns IP addresses and other network settings to devices. It removes manual configuration.

questions.q: What is NAT?
questions.a: NAT (Network Address Translation) converts private IP addresses into a public IP address. It lets many devices share one public IP address.

questions.q: What is the difference between a switch and a router?
questions.a: A switch connects devices within the same network. A router connects different networks and forwards data between them.

questions.q: What is a MAC address?
questions.a: A MAC address is a unique physical address assigned to a network card (NIC). It is used for communication inside the local network.

questions.q: What is ping?
questions.a: Ping is a network utility that checks connectivity between two devices. It also measures the response time.

questions.q: What is traceroute?
questions.a: Traceroute shows the path packets take to reach a destination. It helps find where network delays or failures happen.

questions.q: What are nslookup and dig?
questions.a: Both are DNS lookup tools. nslookup quickly resolves a name to an IP address; dig gives detailed DNS query results and is preferred for troubleshooting.

questions.q: What is the difference between /etc/resolv.conf and /etc/hosts?
questions.a: /etc/resolv.conf stores the DNS server addresses the system queries. /etc/hosts maps names to IP addresses locally and is checked before DNS.

questions.q: What are the 7 layers of the OSI model?
questions.a: 1. Physical, 2. Data Link, 3. Network, 4. Transport, 5. Session, 6. Presentation, 7. Application.

questions.q: What are the common port numbers?
questions.a: 22 - SSH, 21 - FTP, 53 - DNS, 80 - HTTP, 443 - HTTPS, 143 - IMAP, 3389 - RDP, 161 - SNMP, 2049 - NFS.

questions.q: What is a port number?
questions.a: A port number identifies a specific service or application on a device. It directs network traffic to the correct application.

questions.q: What is RIP?
questions.a: RIP is a distance-vector routing protocol. It chooses the best route based on hop count.

questions.q: What are OSPF and IGRP?
questions.a: OSPF is a link-state routing protocol. IGRP is Cisco's distance-vector routing protocol.

questions.q: What is the main DNS configuration file?
questions.a: On RHEL-based systems running BIND, the main DNS server configuration file is /etc/named.conf.

questions.q: Why do we need subnetting?
questions.a: Subnetting divides a network into smaller networks. It improves IP address management, performance, and security.

questions.q: What is a VLAN?
questions.a: A VLAN divides one physical network into multiple logical networks. Devices in different VLANs cannot communicate without a router.

questions.q: What are the classes of IP addresses?
questions.a: The five classes are A, B, C, D, and E. Classes A, B, and C are used for host addressing, D is for multicast, and E is experimental.

questions.q: What is the network ID of 72.59.120.10/25?
questions.a: A /25 mask is 255.255.255.128, so the network ID is 72.59.120.0. Usable host addresses run from 72.59.120.1 to 72.59.120.126.

questions.q: What is the difference between private and public IP addresses?
questions.a: A private IP is used inside a local network and is not reachable from the internet. A public IP is assigned by the ISP and is used to communicate on the internet.

questions.q: What is the difference between HTTP and HTTPS?
questions.a: HTTP transfers data without encryption. HTTPS encrypts data using SSL/TLS, so the communication is secure.

questions.q: What is Active Directory?
questions.a: Active Directory is Microsoft's directory service. It manages users, computers, groups, and permissions in a Windows network.

questions.q: How do you configure a switch?
questions.a: Assign a hostname and a management IP, configure VLANs, and enable the required ports. Always save the configuration after changes.

questions.q: What is a network? What are LAN, MAN and WAN?
questions.a: A network is a group of connected devices that communicate and share data or resources. LAN covers a small local area like an office, MAN covers a city-level area, and WAN covers a large geographical area.

questions.q: What is the TCP/IP model and how is it different from OSI?
questions.a: TCP/IP commonly uses four layers: Link, Internet, Transport and Application. OSI is a seven-layer reference model. OSI Physical plus Data Link maps to TCP/IP Link, OSI Network maps to Internet, OSI Transport maps to Transport, and the upper OSI layers map to Application.

questions.q: What is ARP?
questions.a: ARP maps an IPv4 address to a MAC address on the local network. Linux uses it when it knows the next-hop IP and needs that device's MAC address. Check the neighbor cache with ip neigh.

questions.q: What is Ethernet and what is a frame?
questions.a: Ethernet is a common LAN technology. A frame is the Layer-2 data unit that carries fields such as source MAC, destination MAC and payload. Switches forward Ethernet frames using MAC addresses.

questions.q: How does a switch forward frames?
questions.a: A switch learns which source MAC address is connected to each port and stores that in its MAC address table. It forwards a frame to the port matching the destination MAC. If the destination is unknown, it may flood the frame to other ports.

questions.q: How does a router forward packets?
questions.a: A router checks the destination IP address, looks up the best matching route in its routing table, and forwards the packet to the selected next hop or interface. Routers work mainly at Layer 3.

questions.q: Explain the TCP 3-way handshake.
questions.a: The client sends SYN, the server replies with SYN-ACK, and the client sends ACK. After these three steps, TCP connection state is established and application data can be exchanged.

questions.q: What is the difference between a static route and a default route?
questions.a: A static route is manually configured for a specific destination. A default route is used only when no more specific route matches. View both with ip route.

questions.q: What are eth0, ens33, enp0s3 and lo?
questions.a: They are network interface names. eth0 is the traditional style, ens33 and enp0s3 are predictable names, and lo is the loopback interface. Check the real names on a system with ip a. The loopback interface commonly uses 127.0.0.1/8 for IPv4.

questions.q: How do you configure IP address, gateway and DNS on Linux?
questions.a: The exact method depends on the distribution and network manager. On NetworkManager systems, use nmcli or nmtui for persistent configuration. Temporary testing can use ip addr and ip route, but those changes do not survive reboot unless saved in the system's network configuration.

questions.q: What are nmcli and nmtui?
questions.a: NetworkManager manages network connections. nmcli is its command-line interface, and nmtui is its terminal menu interface. Examples are nmcli device status and nmcli connection show.

questions.q: How does SSH work?
questions.a: SSH provides encrypted remote login and secure transport, normally on TCP port 22 unless configured otherwise. The client establishes an encrypted connection to the server and authenticates with a password or SSH keys. Key-based authentication is common in production.

questions.q: A Linux server has no network. What do you check first?
questions.a: Troubleshoot layer by layer: check link and IP with ip link and ip a, routes with ip route, then gateway reachability, public IP reachability, DNS, listening ports, firewall rules and logs. A typical sequence is ip a, ip route, ping gateway, ping 8.8.8.8, dig example.com, ss -tulnp, then firewall and logs.

questions.q: What is a proxy server? Forward proxy vs reverse proxy?
questions.a: A proxy is an intermediary between a client and a destination service. A forward proxy commonly represents clients and can provide filtering, logging or caching. A reverse proxy commonly represents backend servers and routes client requests to them.

questions.q: What is a VPN?
questions.a: A VPN creates an authenticated and encrypted tunnel over another network, often the Internet. It lets a remote user or another network reach private resources securely. Common types are remote-access VPN and site-to-site VPN.

questions.q: What is NIC bonding or teaming?
questions.a: Bonding or teaming combines multiple network interfaces into one logical connection for redundancy, load distribution or both. The exact benefit depends on the bonding mode and switch configuration. Common modes include active-backup and LACP (802.3ad) where supported.

questions.q: What is a Linux bridge?
questions.a: A Linux bridge connects Layer-2 segments and forwards Ethernet frames using MAC learning, similar to a switch. It is common in virtualization to connect virtual machine interfaces to a physical LAN.

questions.q: What are the basic IPv6 address types?
questions.a: Common types are global unicast, link-local (fe80::/10), unique local (fc00::/7), multicast (ff00::/8) and loopback (::1). IPv6 does not use broadcast; it uses multicast and neighbor discovery instead. 2001:db8::/32 is reserved for documentation examples.

questions.q: How do you troubleshoot DNS?
questions.a: First separate IP connectivity from name resolution. If ping 8.8.8.8 works but ping example.com fails, suspect DNS. Check /etc/resolv.conf or resolvectl status, then test directly with dig example.com or nslookup example.com and verify the DNS server is reachable.

questions.q: DHCP is not assigning an IP. What do you check?
questions.a: Check whether the interface is up, the DHCP client is running, the VLAN or switch path is correct, and the DHCP server is available. If the client and server are on different subnets, also check the DHCP relay. NetworkManager and DHCP client logs can show the failed DORA exchange.

questions.q: How do you check networking logs in Linux?
questions.a: On systemd systems, use journalctl. For NetworkManager, use journalctl -u NetworkManager, and for current boot messages use journalctl -b. Example: journalctl -u NetworkManager --since '10 min ago'.

questions.q: How do you troubleshoot a network service?
questions.a: Confirm the service is running, listening on the expected address and port, reachable locally and remotely, and allowed by firewall or SELinux. Useful checks are systemctl status ssh, ss -lntp | grep :22, curl or nc tests, firewall rules and service logs.

questions.q: A port is listening locally but not reachable remotely. Why?
questions.a: A local listening socket only means the service is bound on that machine. Remote access can still fail because of firewall rules, routing, cloud security groups, ACLs, SELinux or the service binding only to localhost. Compare ss output on the server with a remote nc or curl test.

questions.q: Ping works but SSH does not. What would you check?
questions.a: Ping only proves basic IP/ICMP reachability; SSH uses TCP. Check that sshd is running, TCP/22 is listening, firewall and routing allow TCP/22, SSH is bound to the right address, and authentication is valid. Use systemctl status ssh or sshd, ss -lntp | grep :22, firewall-cmd --list-all and ssh -v user@server.

questions.q: How do you check disk space and directory sizes?
questions.a: df -h shows used and free space per mounted filesystem. du -sh /path shows how much one directory uses, and du -sh * sizes everything in the current directory.

questions.q: What does mounting a filesystem mean?
questions.a: Attaching a filesystem - from a partition, disk or network share - onto a directory in the tree, for example mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data. Everything written under that directory then goes to the device.

questions.q: What is /etc/fstab?
questions.a: The table of filesystems mounted automatically at boot: device (best given as UUID=...), mount point, filesystem type, options, and dump/fsck fields. A broken line can drop the boot into emergency mode, so always test edits with mount -a.

questions.q: ext4, XFS and Btrfs in one line each?
questions.a: ext4 is the mature journaling default on many distros. XFS is tuned for large files and parallel workloads and is the RHEL default. Btrfs adds copy-on-write, snapshots and built-in volume features.

questions.q: What is swap?
questions.a: Disk space the kernel uses as overflow memory when RAM runs out, and for hibernation. swapon --show lists active swap; a new swap area is prepared with mkswap and activated with swapon.

questions.q: What is LVM and why use it?
questions.a: Logical Volume Manager inserts a flexible layer between disks and filesystems: physical volumes (disks) join a volume group, from which logical volumes are carved out. The benefit is resizing, snapshots and moving volumes without repartitioning.

questions.q: What does fsck do, and when does it run?
questions.a: fsck checks and repairs filesystem consistency, and it must run on an UNMOUNTED filesystem. At boot it runs automatically when a filesystem is marked dirty or has passed its mount-count limit.

questions.q: The disk is full - how do you find what is filling it?
questions.a: df -h shows which filesystem is full, then du -xh --max-depth=1 / | sort -h finds the biggest directories; /var/log and package caches are common culprits. Files that are deleted but still open keep holding space - find them with lsof +L1.

questions.q: What is an inode?
questions.a: The filesystem's record for a file: permissions, owner, timestamps and pointers to the data blocks - everything except the name, which lives in directory entries. Running out of inodes makes a disk report full even with blocks free; check with df -i.

questions.q: How do you partition and format a disk from the command line?
questions.a: Identify the disk with lsblk, partition it with fdisk /dev/sdX or parted, format the new partition with mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdX1, then mount it. Every step destroys data if you pick the wrong disk - double-check the device name first.

questions.q: What is a partition?
questions.a: A partition is a logical section of a storage device. It lets one disk be divided into multiple independent areas.

questions.q: What is the difference between MBR and GPT?
questions.a: MBR supports disks up to 2 TB and a maximum of four primary partitions. GPT supports very large disks and many more partitions, and it is the modern standard.

questions.q: What is a file system?
questions.a: A file system is the method an operating system uses to store, organize, and manage files on a storage device. Examples are ext4, XFS, and Btrfs.

questions.q: Which file system does RHEL 7 use by default?
questions.a: RHEL 7 uses XFS as its default file system.

questions.q: How do you check free memory?
questions.a: Use free -h to see RAM and swap usage in human-readable form.

questions.q: How do you mount and unmount a directory?
questions.a: Use mount to attach a filesystem to a directory: mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data. Use umount /mnt/data to detach it safely before removing the device.

questions.q: How do you increase a disk partition?
questions.a: First grow the partition itself (with growpart or fdisk), then expand the filesystem: resize2fs for ext4 or xfs_growfs for XFS. With LVM, use lvextend and then the same filesystem resize step.

questions.q: What are the common LVM commands?
questions.a: pvcreate prepares a disk as a physical volume, vgcreate builds a volume group, lvcreate carves out a logical volume, lvextend grows it, and lvreduce shrinks it.

questions.q: What is the shebang line?
questions.a: The first line of a script, like #!/bin/bash, that tells the kernel which interpreter should execute the file. Without it, your current shell interprets the script instead.

questions.q: How do you make a script executable and run it?
questions.a: chmod +x script.sh, then run it with an explicit path: ./script.sh. The current directory is deliberately not in PATH, so the ./ is required. bash script.sh works without the execute bit.

questions.q: How do variables and command substitution work?
questions.a: name=value sets a variable (no spaces around =); $name or ${name} reads it. $(command) captures a command's output, as in today=$(date +%F). Quote expansions - "$name" - so values with spaces survive.

questions.q: How do you read command-line arguments in a script?
questions.a: $1, $2... are the positional parameters, $# is their count, $@ is all of them and $0 is the script's own name. Validate them early: [ $# -lt 1 ] && { echo "usage: $0 FILE"; exit 1; }.

questions.q: What is the exit status and what is $?
questions.a: Every command returns 0 on success and a non-zero code on failure; $? holds the last command's status. Writing if command; then tests it directly, and well-behaved scripts end with exit 0 on success.

questions.q: Give one example each of if, for and while in bash.
questions.a: if [ -f /etc/passwd ]; then echo yes; fi --- for f in *.log; do echo "$f"; done --- while read -r line; do echo "$line"; done < file. The [ ] command runs tests: -f file exists, -z empty string, = string equality, -eq numeric equality.

questions.q: What does set -euo pipefail do?
questions.a: Strict mode: -e exits the script at the first failing command, -u treats unset variables as errors, and -o pipefail makes a pipeline fail if ANY stage fails, not just the last. It surfaces bugs early and is expected in serious scripts.

questions.q: What is the difference between $* and $@?
questions.a: Both expand to all arguments, but quoted "$@" keeps each argument as a separate word while "$*" joins them into one. For looping over arguments, "$@" is almost always the right choice.

questions.q: How do you schedule a script to run regularly?
questions.a: With cron: crontab -e, then a line like 0 2 * * * /home/akash/backup.sh (minute hour day month weekday). systemd timers are the modern alternative when you need dependencies and journal logging.

questions.q: How do you debug a shell script?
questions.a: bash -x script.sh prints every command as it executes; you can wrap a suspect block in set -x / set +x. Echo key variables along the way and check failures with echo $?.

questions.q: What is a shell script?
questions.a: A shell script is a text file that contains a sequence of Linux commands. It is used to automate repetitive tasks.

questions.q: Why do we use shell scripting?
questions.a: Shell scripting saves time by automating manual work. It makes tasks repeatable and reduces human error.

questions.q: What happens when a Linux machine boots?
questions.a: The firmware (BIOS/UEFI) runs the bootloader (GRUB); GRUB loads the kernel and initramfs; the kernel mounts the root filesystem and starts PID 1 (systemd); systemd then starts units until the default target - multi-user or graphical - is reached.

questions.q: What is systemd and what is a unit?
questions.a: systemd is PID 1, the init system that starts and supervises everything else. A unit is a resource it manages: .service (daemons), .socket, .timer, .mount, .path and .target (boot stages that group units).

questions.q: systemctl basics: start, stop, enable?
questions.a: systemctl start/stop/restart name controls a service right now. systemctl enable name links it to start at boot (disable removes the link). systemctl enable --now name does both at once, and status name shows its state plus recent log lines.

questions.q: What is the difference between systemctl enable and systemctl start?
questions.a: start changes the running system only - the effect is gone after reboot. enable only creates the boot-time symlink and does not start anything now. systemctl enable --now combines both.

questions.q: How do you read a service's logs?
questions.a: journalctl -u name shows one unit's logs; journalctl -f follows new entries live; journalctl -b limits to the current boot; journalctl -p err shows errors and worse. Traditional text logs still live under /var/log.

questions.q: Where do unit files live, and how do you edit one safely?
questions.a: Vendor units live in /usr/lib/systemd/system (or /lib/systemd/system on Debian/Ubuntu); local and custom units live in /etc/systemd/system and override them. Edit with systemctl edit name, which creates a drop-in instead of touching vendor files, then run systemctl daemon-reload.

questions.q: What is a target?
questions.a: A systemd boot stage that groups units - the successor of runlevels. multi-user.target is the text-mode server state and graphical.target adds the desktop. systemctl get-default and set-default control which one boots; systemctl isolate switches immediately.

questions.q: How do you create your own service?
questions.a: Write /etc/systemd/system/myservice.service with a [Unit] section (Description, After=network.target), a [Service] section (ExecStart=/path/to/command, optionally Restart=on-failure) and an [Install] section (WantedBy=multi-user.target). Then systemctl daemon-reload and systemctl enable --now myservice.

questions.q: How do you see why boot was slow or what failed?
questions.a: systemd-analyze prints the total boot time; systemd-analyze blame ranks units by startup time; systemctl --failed lists failed units; journalctl -b -p err shows this boot's errors.

questions.q: What is the difference between a systemd timer and cron?
questions.a: A timer unit triggers a service on a schedule and adds dependencies, journal logging and catch-up of missed runs (Persistent=true). cron is simpler and available everywhere; timers integrate with the rest of systemd.

questions.q: What is a service?
questions.a: A service is a program that runs in the background to provide specific functionality. Examples include the SSH, Apache, and MySQL services.

questions.q: What is the difference between systemctl and service?
questions.a: systemctl manages services on systemd-based systems, which covers most modern distros. service is the older SysVinit command that still works for compatibility on many systems.

questions.q: What is GRUB?
questions.a: GRUB (Grand Unified Bootloader) is the Linux bootloader. It loads the kernel into memory and starts the operating system.

questions.q: What is journald?
questions.a: journald is the logging service of systemd. It collects and stores system and service logs, which you read with journalctl.

questions.q: How do you host a web server on Linux?
questions.a: Install a web server like Apache or Nginx with the package manager, place the website files in its web root (for example /var/www/html), then start and enable the service with systemctl.

questions.q: What are the most important log locations?
questions.a: The systemd journal (read it with journalctl), /var/log/syslog or /var/log/messages for general logs, /var/log/auth.log or /var/log/secure for logins and sudo, and per-service files like /var/log/nginx/. Kernel messages appear in the journal and /var/log/kern.log.

questions.q: How do you see who is logged in and the login history?
questions.a: who or w shows current sessions. last lists past logins from the wtmp database, and lastb lists FAILED attempts from btmp. journalctl _COMM=sshd filters SSH events.

questions.q: What is the cron time format?
questions.a: Five fields - minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week - followed by the command. A * means 'every'. So 30 3 * * 0 runs at 03:30 every Sunday. Shortcuts like @daily and @reboot also exist.

questions.q: crontab -e versus /etc/crontab versus /etc/cron.d?
questions.a: crontab -e edits the current user's personal crontab, whose lines have no user field. /etc/crontab and files in /etc/cron.d are system-wide and include a user field between the schedule and the command. Scripts dropped in cron.daily, cron.weekly and cron.monthly run on those schedules.

questions.q: A cron job did not run - how do you debug it?
questions.a: Check the log with grep CRON /var/log/syslog or journalctl -u cron, confirm the cron service is running, and remember cron uses a minimal environment: use absolute paths, set PATH explicitly, and capture errors with >> /tmp/job.log 2>&1.

questions.q: What is a Linux firewall and which tools manage it?
questions.a: It filters network traffic by rules. The kernel framework is nftables (iptables is the legacy one); friendly front-ends are ufw on Ubuntu (ufw allow 22, ufw enable) and firewalld on RHEL (firewall-cmd).

questions.q: How do you harden SSH on a server?
questions.a: Use key-based login and disable passwords (PasswordAuthentication no), disable direct root login (PermitRootLogin no), optionally restrict users with AllowUsers, keep the system patched, and add fail2ban to slow brute-force attacks.

questions.q: What are SSH keys and how do you set them up?
questions.a: A key pair: the private key stays on your machine (~/.ssh/id_ed25519) and the public key goes on the server (~/.ssh/authorized_keys). Create them with ssh-keygen -t ed25519 and install the public key with ssh-copy-id user@host - after that, logins need no password.

questions.q: What are SELinux and AppArmor?
questions.a: Mandatory Access Control systems that confine even root-owned processes by policy. SELinux (RHEL family) works with labels - check getenforce and the audit log for denials. AppArmor (Ubuntu, SUSE) confines programs by path-based profiles - check aa-status.

questions.q: How do you investigate high load or memory trouble?
questions.a: uptime shows the load average - compare it with the CPU count. top or htop shows per-process CPU and memory, free -h shows RAM and swap usage, vmstat 1 shows trends, and dmesg -T reveals kernel events such as OOM-killer kills.

questions.q: What is the difference between SELinux and a firewall?
questions.a: SELinux controls access inside the operating system - files, processes, and resources. A firewall controls incoming and outgoing network traffic.

questions.q: What is firewalld?
questions.a: firewalld is the default firewall management service on RHEL-based systems. It manages rules dynamically with zones, using the firewall-cmd command.

questions.q: What is the difference between iptables and a firewall?
questions.a: A firewall is the security system that filters network traffic. iptables is the classic command-line tool for writing those rules; modern systems use nftables instead.

questions.q: How do you add an iptables rule?
questions.a: Use iptables -A to append a rule, for example: iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT allows SSH traffic. Save the rules afterwards so they survive a reboot.

questions.q: What is Anacron?
questions.a: Anacron runs scheduled tasks that were missed because the system was powered off. It is meant for machines that do not run all the time, like laptops.

questions.q: What is the difference between Cron and Anacron?
questions.a: Cron runs jobs at exact times and assumes the machine is always on. Anacron catches up on missed jobs when the system comes back, working with day-level schedules.

questions.q: Your Linux system has malware. What will you do?
questions.a: Disconnect the system from the network, identify and remove the infected files, patch and update the system, and restore from a clean backup if needed. Review logs to find how it entered.

questions.q: The server is down. How will you troubleshoot?
questions.a: Check power and network first, then whether the server is reachable with ping. Check services, logs, disk space, CPU, and memory. Restart the failed service and verify the application works.

questions.q: SSH is not working. How will you troubleshoot?
questions.a: Check network connectivity, confirm sshd is running with systemctl status sshd, verify the firewall allows port 22, and review the SSH logs.

questions.q: A service is not starting. What will you check?
questions.a: Check systemctl status for the error, read its logs with journalctl -u, and verify the configuration file for mistakes.

questions.q: The server cannot access the internet. What will you verify?
questions.a: Check the IP address, gateway, and DNS settings, then test step by step: ping the gateway, an external IP, and a domain name.

questions.q: Users cannot log in. What will you check?
questions.a: Check whether the account is locked or expired, the password, permissions, and the authentication logs. Also verify that SSH or login services are running.

questions.q: A filesystem became read-only. What could be the reason?
questions.a: Usually filesystem corruption or disk errors - the kernel remounts it read-only to protect data. Check dmesg and disk health, then run fsck from a rescue environment.

questions.q: The server does not boot after a restart. What will you do?
questions.a: Check the bootloader (GRUB), the kernel, and the boot logs. Boot into rescue mode if needed, identify the failed component, and repair it.

questions.q: How do you take a backup in Linux?
questions.a: Use tar for archives and rsync to sync files to another disk or server. Keep backups in a separate, secure location and test that restores work.

questions.q: What is the difference between backup and synchronization?
questions.a: A backup is a recoverable copy with a separate destination, retention and restore testing. Synchronization mirrors changes, and a mirrored copy can also mirror accidental deletion. Use rsync or tar carefully, verify checksums and test restores.

questions.q: What is the difference between rsync and cp?
questions.a: cp copies files each time, while rsync compares source and destination and transfers only the changes. rsync is better for repeated backups and remote synchronization. It can also preserve permissions and show a dry run first.

questions.q: Why is rsync --dry-run important?
questions.a: --dry-run shows what rsync would change without changing the destination. It is especially useful before using --delete, which can remove files from the destination. Always preview destructive sync jobs.

questions.q: How do you create, list and extract a tar backup?
questions.a: Create a compressed archive with tar -czf backup.tar.gz /path. List contents with tar -tzf backup.tar.gz. Extract into a restore directory with tar -xzf backup.tar.gz -C /restore/.

questions.q: Why should backups have checksums?
questions.a: A checksum such as sha256sum proves that the backup file was not corrupted during copy or storage. Verify the checksum before relying on the backup for a restore.

questions.q: What makes a backup plan production-ready?
questions.a: A production backup plan needs retention, a separate destination, monitoring and regular restore testing. A backup that has never been restored is not fully trusted.

questions.q: What is the difference between apt and dpkg?
questions.a: apt works with repositories and resolves dependencies, so it is normally the right tool for installing and upgrading packages on Ubuntu/Debian. dpkg is the lower-level tool for installing or inspecting individual .deb files. Use apt first when possible.

questions.q: What is the difference between apt update and apt upgrade?
questions.a: apt update refreshes the package index from repositories. apt upgrade installs available upgrades for installed packages. Update tells apt what is available; upgrade applies the changes.

questions.q: What is the difference between apt remove, purge and autoremove?
questions.a: remove uninstalls a package but can leave configuration files. purge removes the package and its configuration where applicable. autoremove removes dependencies that are no longer needed.

questions.q: How do you inspect a package before installing it?
questions.a: Use apt search to find packages, apt show for details, and apt policy to see installed and candidate versions plus repositories. These commands do not install anything.

questions.q: How do you inspect installed .deb packages with dpkg?
questions.a: Use dpkg -l to list installed packages, dpkg -L package to list files from a package, and dpkg -S /path/file to find which package owns a file.

questions.q: Why is apt usually preferred over dpkg -i?
questions.a: dpkg -i installs a local .deb but does not resolve repository dependencies by itself. apt understands repositories and dependencies, so it is safer for normal package installation.

questions.q: What are RAID, NFS, Samba and swap used for?
questions.a: RAID combines disks for redundancy or performance depending on the level, but it does not replace backups. NFS is common for Linux network shares, Samba provides SMB/CIFS shares for Windows clients, and swap is disk-backed memory overflow. Monitor swap as a sign of memory pressure.

questions.q: What are common RAID levels?
questions.a: RAID 0 stripes data for performance without redundancy. RAID 1 mirrors disks. RAID 5 uses distributed parity and needs at least three disks. RAID 6 uses double parity, and RAID 10 combines mirroring and striping.

questions.q: How do you check Linux software RAID status?
questions.a: Check /proc/mdstat for a quick status and rebuild progress. Use mdadm --detail /dev/md0 for detailed information about the array and member disks.

questions.q: What is the difference between NFS and Samba?
questions.a: NFS is commonly used for Linux and Unix network file shares. Samba provides SMB/CIFS shares, commonly for Windows clients. Both share files over the network, but they use different protocols.

questions.q: What is swap and when is it a warning sign?
questions.a: Swap is disk-backed virtual memory used when RAM is under pressure. Some swap use can be normal, but constant heavy swapping usually means the server needs more RAM or a memory-heavy process needs attention.

questions.q: How do you mount an NFS or SMB share?
questions.a: For NFS, use mount -t nfs server:/share /mnt/share. For SMB/CIFS, use mount -t cifs //server/share /mnt/share with the required username option. Verify the mount with df -h.

questions.q: Why can a bad /etc/fstab entry stop Linux from booting normally?
questions.a: During boot, systemd mounts filesystems from /etc/fstab. A missing disk, wrong UUID or bad mount option can make boot drop into emergency mode. Check lsblk -f and blkid, fix the entry, then test with mount -a before rebooting.

questions.q: What is the normal Linux boot sequence?
questions.a: The broad sequence is BIOS or UEFI, GRUB, kernel and initramfs, systemd, then services and login. Knowing this order helps isolate whether the problem is firmware, bootloader, kernel, filesystem or service related.

questions.q: How do you reset a forgotten root password on many RHEL-family systems?
questions.a: Interrupt GRUB, add rd.break to the kernel line, boot, remount /sysroot read-write with mount -o remount,rw /sysroot, chroot into /sysroot, run passwd, then touch /.autorelabel so SELinux relabels on reboot. Exit cleanly and reboot. Use this only on systems you are authorized to administer.

questions.q: What is the difference between rescue and emergency mode?
questions.a: Rescue mode starts more of the system and usually mounts filesystems, while emergency mode starts a very minimal environment for severe recovery. Use emergency mode when normal rescue mode cannot mount or start required pieces.

questions.q: How do you test fstab changes before rebooting?
questions.a: After editing /etc/fstab, run mount -a as root. This tries the configured mounts without rebooting and catches many wrong UUID, filesystem or mount-point problems early.

questions.q: When should you use fsck?
questions.a: Use fsck to check or repair a filesystem only when it is unmounted and the procedure is appropriate for that filesystem. Do not run fsck on a mounted filesystem; boot from rescue media if the root filesystem needs repair.

questions.q: How do you troubleshoot a slow Linux server?
questions.a: Start with evidence instead of killing processes blindly. Check load and CPU with uptime/top, memory and swap with free -h, disk I/O with iostat or pidstat, then correlate with application logs. Identify the responsible process and follow the change procedure.

questions.q: What does load average mean?
questions.a: Load average shows how many tasks are running or waiting, averaged over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. Compare it with the number of CPU cores; a high sustained load means the system may be overloaded or waiting on I/O.

questions.q: How do you find a high-CPU process?
questions.a: Use top for a live view, or ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head for a quick list. Identify what the process is and why it is busy before stopping it.

questions.q: How do you check memory pressure?
questions.a: Use free -h to see RAM and swap usage. If available memory is low and swap is heavily used, find the memory-heavy process with top or ps aux --sort=-%mem | head.

questions.q: How do you investigate disk I/O problems?
questions.a: Use iostat -xz to see device utilization and latency, and pidstat -d to identify per-process I/O. High await or utilization can explain slow applications.

questions.q: What do you check when a filesystem is full?
questions.a: Use df -h to find the full filesystem and df -i to check inode exhaustion. Then use du -xhd1 on the filesystem to find large directories before deleting anything.

questions.q: What is the difference between rsyslog and logrotate?
questions.a: rsyslog collects, filters and forwards log messages. logrotate rotates, compresses and retains old logs so they do not fill the filesystem. Use journalctl or the right /var/log file to investigate, and logrotate -d to preview rotation safely.

questions.q: Where are common Linux logs stored?
questions.a: Systemd systems use the journal, read with journalctl. Traditional logs often live under /var/log, such as /var/log/messages on RHEL-family systems and /var/log/syslog on Debian-family systems.

questions.q: How do you read logs for one service?
questions.a: Use journalctl -u service-name. Add -f to follow live logs or --since '1 hour ago' to limit the time range. Example: journalctl -u nginx -f.

questions.q: How do you create a test log message?
questions.a: Use logger 'message'. It writes a test message through the system logging path, which helps verify rsyslog or journal configuration.

questions.q: How do you test logrotate safely?
questions.a: Use logrotate -d /etc/logrotate.conf for a dry run. It shows what would rotate without changing files. Force rotation only when you understand the impact.

questions.q: How can logs fill a disk and how do you prevent it?
questions.a: High-volume application or system logs can consume all space in /var or /var/log. logrotate retention, compression and correct application log levels help prevent it. Check space with df -h and large directories with du.

questions.q: How do you troubleshoot a 502 from Nginx or Apache?
questions.a: Validate the web server config, check the service, confirm the upstream application is listening, and read the error log. Useful checks are nginx -t or apachectl -t, systemctl status, ss -tuln, curl and the site error logs.

questions.q: What is the difference between Apache and Nginx?
questions.a: Both can serve web content and act as reverse proxies. Nginx is often used as a lightweight reverse proxy and static web server, while Apache is a mature web server with flexible modules. The right choice depends on the application and team standards.

questions.q: Why should you test web server config before reload?
questions.a: A syntax error can stop the service during reload or restart. Use nginx -t for Nginx and apachectl -t or httpd -t for Apache before applying configuration.

questions.q: What is a virtual host or server block?
questions.a: It is the configuration that maps a site name, port and document root or proxy target to a website or application. Apache calls it a virtual host; Nginx commonly calls it a server block.

questions.q: How do you check whether web ports are listening?
questions.a: Use ss -tuln on the server and look for ports 80 and 443. Then test locally with curl -I and remotely from another machine to separate service binding from firewall or routing problems.

questions.q: What do common 4xx and 5xx HTTP errors mean?
questions.a: 4xx errors are client-side or request-related, such as 403 forbidden or 404 not found. 5xx errors are server-side or upstream-related, such as 500, 502 and 503. Check logs to find the exact cause.

questions.q: An application cannot connect to MySQL. What do you check?
questions.a: Check the MySQL service, listening address and port, credentials, database name, user privileges and database logs before changing application code. For backup and restore practice, use mysqldump and a separate test database. Never expose production passwords in commands or docs.

questions.q: Why might MySQL be called mysql or mysqld in systemctl?
questions.a: The service name depends on the distribution and package. Ubuntu/Debian often use mysql, while many RHEL-family packages use mysqld or mariadb. Check installed services with systemctl status mysql, mysqld or mariadb.

questions.q: How should you create a MySQL application user?
questions.a: Create a user for the required host and grant only the privileges the application needs. Avoid using root for applications, and never place production passwords in shared docs or command history.

questions.q: How do you list databases and tables?
questions.a: Connect with mysql -u user -p, then use SHOW DATABASES, USE database_name and SHOW TABLES. These commands help confirm that the expected database exists.

questions.q: How do you back up and restore a MySQL database?
questions.a: Use mysqldump -u user -p database_name > backup.sql for a logical backup. Restore into a test database with mysql -u user -p database_name < backup.sql. Test restores regularly.

questions.q: How do you check whether MySQL is responding?
questions.a: Use systemctl status for the service, ss -lntp for the listener, and mysqladmin ping with valid credentials. Also review the database error log if the service will not start.

questions.q: chmod looks correct but a web app still gets Permission denied. What do you check?
questions.a: Check SELinux context and AVC denials before changing broad permissions or disabling SELinux. Use ls -Z, restorecon, semanage fcontext where appropriate, and ausearch -m AVC. Also review ACLs, sudo rules and fail2ban status when relevant.

questions.q: What are SELinux enforcing, permissive and disabled modes?
questions.a: Enforcing applies SELinux policy and logs denials. Permissive logs what would be denied but does not block it. Disabled turns SELinux off. Prefer fixing contexts or policy instead of disabling SELinux.

questions.q: What is an SELinux context?
questions.a: An SELinux context labels files, processes and ports with security information. A web server can be denied even when Unix permissions look correct. Use ls -Z to view contexts and restorecon to restore expected labels.

questions.q: How do you find SELinux denials?
questions.a: Use ausearch -m AVC -ts recent or check audit logs. AVC messages show what was denied and help you choose a targeted fix instead of disabling SELinux.

questions.q: Why should sudoers be edited with visudo?
questions.a: visudo checks sudoers syntax before saving, reducing the chance of locking yourself out of sudo. Grant least privilege instead of broad ALL rules.

questions.q: What are ACLs in Linux?
questions.a: ACLs extend normal owner/group/other permissions by allowing specific users or groups to have their own permissions. Use getfacl to view ACLs and setfacl to change them.

questions.q: What does fail2ban do?
questions.a: fail2ban watches logs for repeated authentication failures and can temporarily block offending sources using firewall rules. Check jail status with fail2ban-client status sshd.

questions.q: What is the difference between local Linux accounts and LDAP/Active Directory accounts?
questions.a: Local accounts exist only on one machine, while LDAP or Active Directory provides centrally managed identity. Linux can integrate through SSSD and realmd, often using Kerberos for authentication. Use id, getent, klist and SSSD tools when troubleshooting.

questions.q: What is the difference between LDAP and Active Directory?
questions.a: LDAP is a directory access protocol. Active Directory is Microsoft's directory service and commonly uses LDAP plus Kerberos and other services. Linux can authenticate against either with the right integration.

questions.q: What is Kerberos used for?
questions.a: Kerberos provides ticket-based authentication, commonly in Active Directory environments. Commands like kinit request a ticket and klist shows current tickets.

questions.q: What are SSSD and realmd?
questions.a: SSSD connects Linux authentication and identity lookup to directory services such as LDAP or AD. realmd helps discover and join supported domains. Together they allow centralized logins on Linux.

questions.q: How do you test whether a directory user resolves on Linux?
questions.a: Use id username and getent passwd username. If the user does not resolve, check SSSD, domain join status, DNS and network connectivity.

questions.q: Why is time important for AD or Kerberos login?
questions.a: Kerberos is sensitive to clock skew. If the Linux server clock is too far from the domain controller, authentication can fail. Check timedatectl and chrony synchronization.

questions.q: What is the difference between monitoring and troubleshooting?
questions.a: Monitoring collects metrics, checks availability, shows trends and sends alerts. Troubleshooting finds the reason behind the alert using Linux tools such as top, vmstat, iostat, pidstat and logs. Zabbix, Grafana and Nagios help detect change; they do not replace diagnosis.

questions.q: What are Zabbix, Grafana and Nagios used for?
questions.a: Zabbix collects metrics and sends alerts, Grafana builds dashboards and visualizations, and Nagios runs host/service checks with plugins. They can work together or separately depending on the environment.

questions.q: What is the difference between metrics, logs and alerts?
questions.a: Metrics are numeric measurements over time, logs are event records, and alerts notify when a rule or threshold is triggered. Good troubleshooting uses all three together.

questions.q: How do you check a monitoring agent?
questions.a: Check the agent service, such as systemctl status zabbix-agent, then inspect its logs with journalctl -u zabbix-agent. Also verify the monitoring server is allowed to reach the agent port.

questions.q: What is a Nagios plugin?
questions.a: A Nagios plugin is a small check program that tests a host or service, such as check_ping or check_http. It returns a status that Nagios can alert on.

questions.q: Why should monitoring ports be checked?
questions.a: Dashboards and agents listen on network ports. If the web UI or agent is unreachable, use ss -tuln on the server and a remote curl or nc test to separate service, firewall and routing issues.

questions.q: What are inventory, modules and playbooks in Ansible?
questions.a: Inventory lists the managed hosts, modules perform actions, and YAML playbooks describe the desired state. Good playbooks are repeatable and preferably idempotent, so running them again does not make unnecessary changes.

questions.q: Why is Ansible called agentless?
questions.a: Ansible normally manages hosts over SSH and does not require a permanent agent on each managed Linux server. The control node runs modules against hosts from inventory.

questions.q: What is the difference between an ad-hoc command and a playbook?
questions.a: An ad-hoc command runs one module against selected hosts, such as ansible all -m ping. A playbook is a YAML file that describes an ordered set of tasks and desired state.

questions.q: What does idempotent mean in Ansible?
questions.a: An idempotent playbook can be run repeatedly and only makes changes when the system is not already in the desired state. This is important for safe automation.

questions.q: What does ansible-playbook --check do?
questions.a: --check previews what the playbook would change where supported, without applying the changes. It is useful for review, although not every module supports full check-mode prediction.

questions.q: How can Ansible install a package and start a service?
questions.a: Use the package module to ensure the package is present and the service module to ensure the service is started and enabled. A playbook can apply the same state to many servers.

questions.q: What is the difference between a Docker container and a KVM virtual machine?
questions.a: A Docker container packages an application and shares the host kernel, while KVM runs a full guest operating system using Linux kernel virtualization. Containers are lighter for application deployment; VMs provide a separate OS and stronger isolation boundary.

questions.q: What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?
questions.a: An image is the packaged application template. A container is a running instance created from an image. One image can create many containers.

questions.q: How do you publish a Docker container port?
questions.a: Use docker run -p hostPort:containerPort. For example, docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx maps host port 8080 to container port 80.

questions.q: How do you debug a running container?
questions.a: Use docker logs -f name to follow logs and docker exec -it name sh to open a shell when the image includes one. Also inspect ports and configuration with docker inspect.

questions.q: How do you stop and remove a container?
questions.a: Use docker stop name for a graceful stop and docker rm name to remove a stopped container. Use docker ps -a to see stopped containers.

questions.q: How do you manage KVM virtual machines with virsh?
questions.a: Use virsh list --all to list VMs, virsh start name to start one, virsh shutdown name for a graceful shutdown, and virsh console name for console access when configured.

questions.q: Why is time synchronization important on Linux servers?
questions.a: Accurate time is required for Kerberos/Active Directory, TLS certificate validation, useful logs and distributed systems. Chrony is a common NTP implementation. Check time with timedatectl and synchronization with chronyc tracking or sources.

questions.q: How do you check Linux time and timezone?
questions.a: Use timedatectl. It shows current time, timezone and whether network time synchronization is enabled.

questions.q: How do you set the Linux timezone?
questions.a: Use timedatectl set-timezone with an IANA timezone, such as sudo timedatectl set-timezone Asia/Kolkata. Verify with timedatectl afterward.

questions.q: What is chronyd?
questions.a: chronyd is the daemon for the Chrony NTP implementation. It keeps the system clock synchronized with configured time sources.

questions.q: How do you check chrony synchronization?
questions.a: Use chronyc tracking for offset and synchronization status, and chronyc sources -v for the state of configured time sources.

questions.q: When would you use chronyc makestep?
questions.a: chronyc makestep steps the clock when there is a significant offset and the administrator decides an immediate correction is appropriate. Use caution because time jumps can affect applications and logs.

items.use: Check chrony daemon on many RHEL-family systems.

questions.q: Which AWS services should a Linux administrator know first?
questions.a: Start with EC2 for virtual servers, EBS for disks, VPC/subnets/route tables for networking, security groups for traffic control, IAM for permissions, S3 for object storage and CloudWatch for monitoring. Know how these map to normal Linux admin work.

questions.q: What is EC2?
questions.a: EC2 is AWS's virtual server service. A Linux admin can choose an instance, attach storage, configure networking and connect with SSH, subject to security groups and key access.

questions.q: What is the difference between EBS and S3?
questions.a: EBS provides block storage volumes that attach to EC2 instances like disks. S3 is object storage for files and backups, accessed through APIs or tools such as aws s3 cp and sync.

questions.q: What is a security group?
questions.a: A security group is a virtual firewall attached to AWS resources such as EC2 instances. It controls allowed inbound and outbound traffic by protocol, port and source or destination.

questions.q: What is IAM and why are roles preferred for EC2?
questions.a: IAM controls AWS identity and permissions. An EC2 instance role lets the instance call approved AWS APIs without storing long-term access keys on the server.

questions.q: What is CloudWatch used for?
questions.a: CloudWatch collects AWS metrics, logs and alarms. A Linux admin can use it to monitor EC2 health, EBS performance, logs and alert thresholds.

items.use: Configure a CLI profile; prefer roles/SSO for production where possible.
